title: Evolution and natural selection
note: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a population over generations. Natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, mutation, and nonrandom mating all cause it; only natural selection consistently produces adaptation. Individuals do not evolve; populations do.

read.title: How a population changes
text: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace each reasoned their way to natural selection from a few observations. Individuals in a population vary, and much of that variation is inherited. More offspring are born than can survive. Those whose traits suit the environment tend to survive and reproduce more, so their traits become more common over generations.

Modern biology states the same idea in terms of alleles. A population's gene pool holds all its alleles, and evolution is a change in their frequencies. The Hardy–Weinberg principle describes a population that is not evolving: no selection, no mutation, no migration, a population large enough that chance has no effect, and random mating. Real populations always break some of these conditions, and each break is a cause of evolution.

Natural selection is the only cause that steadily fits organisms to their environment. Genetic drift changes allele frequencies by chance and matters most in small populations, such as those that pass through a bottleneck or are founded by a few colonists. Gene flow moves alleles between populations and tends to make them more alike. Mutation supplies the new alleles that all the other forces act on.
Selection acts on individuals, but it is the population that evolves.
